label: History, not Scripture. Researched by Claude, approved by Seabass (SPIRIT §11).

entries.title: Ulfilas gives the Goths an alphabet and the Bible
entries.body: Ulfilas (c. 311–c. 382) was a bishop and missionary to the Goths. He is credited with creating the Gothic alphabet, 27 letters drawn mostly from Greek with some from Latin, so that the Bible could be written in Gothic. His was the earliest Bible in any Germanic language. The original is lost. The best surviving copy, the "Silver Bible" (Codex Argenteus), was written in silver and gold ink on purple parchment in Italy in the early 500s and is kept at Uppsala University Library.
notes: Uncertain: Britannica says his life "cannot be reconstructed with certainty." It dates the translation to about 350, while other sources say only "before 381." Study of the text suggests a team of translators worked with him.
sources: UNESCO Memory of the World, Codex Argenteus

entries.title: Jerome turns to the Hebrew
entries.body: In 382 Pope Damasus I asked Jerome to revise the Latin Gospels against the best Greek texts. Jerome went further and translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew itself, not from the Greek. His Psalms from the Hebrew date to about 390–398. The work was finished around 405. His Latin Bible, the Vulgate, remained the standard Bible of the West for over a thousand years.
sources: Christianity Today, "405 Jerome completes the Vulgate"

entries.title: Mesrop Mashtots writes Armenian down
entries.body: Armenian had no alphabet good enough to carry the Scriptures. Mesrop Mashtots, a monk, devised one in 405, helped by Sahak (Isaac) the Great, head of the Armenian Church. A school of translators then made the first Armenian Bible from the Greek (c. 410). Mashtots himself translated the New Testament and Proverbs, and later revised the whole text. His alphabet is still used today.
notes: Uncertain: Britannica gives the alphabet as 36 letters in one article and 38 in another. His death is given as 440 or 441.

entries.title: Cyril and Methodius bring the Word to the Slavs
entries.body: In 862 Prince Rostislav of Great Moravia asked the Byzantine emperor for missionaries. The brothers Cyril and Methodius were sent, and from 863 they worked among the Slavs. They devised the Glagolitic script, which later developed into Cyrillic, and translated Scripture and the liturgy into what became Old Church Slavonic. German clergy opposed worship in Slavonic. In 868 Pope Adrian II approved it.
notes: Uncertain: exactly which books the brothers themselves translated is not known. The Gospels and the Psalms were probably first.

entries.title: The first whole Bible in English
entries.body: Under John Wycliffe of Oxford, a group of translators, mostly priests, made the first complete Bible in English, translating from the Latin Vulgate. An early word-for-word version (about 1382) was followed by a plainer, more readable one, finished several years after Wycliffe's death in 1384. In 1407–1409 the Church in England forbade new translations without a bishop's approval, yet over 250 manuscripts survive.
notes: Uncertain: which translators did which parts is disputed, and the dates of the revision are given as 1388 or 1395.
sources: Lincoln College, Oxford: rare Wycliffite Bible digitised

entries.title: Gutenberg prints the Bible
entries.body: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg's workshop printed a Latin Bible in two columns of 42 lines. It is the first complete book still in existence printed in the West with movable type. About 180 copies were made in 1454–55. From then on a Bible no longer needed years of hand-copying.
notes: Honest note: Gutenberg did not invent movable type. Korea's Jikji (1377) is older. His casting method and metal made printing practical in Europe.

entries.title: Luther's New Testament for the German people
entries.body: While hidden at Wartburg Castle, Martin Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in about eleven weeks, using Erasmus's Greek text. After revision with Melanchthon it was printed in September 1522, and a second edition was needed by December. The whole Bible followed in 1534, made with Bugenhagen, Jonas, Cruciger, Melanchthon and others. It helped shape the standard German language.

entries.title: Tyndale: the Word from Greek into English, at the cost of his life
entries.body: William Tyndale translated the New Testament straight from Greek into English, the first to do so. It was printed abroad and smuggled into England in 1526, where it was banned at once. He kept translating while in hiding. He was condemned for heresy and executed at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, in 1536, strangled and then burned. Much of his wording passed into later English Bibles.
notes: Uncertain: Britannica gives 18,000 copies printed by his death in one article and "several thousand" in another. The exact day of his death is uncertain, around early October 1536.

entries.title: William Carey and the Serampore translators
entries.body: William Carey, an English shoemaker turned missionary, went to India in 1793. Working with Indian scholars and his colleagues at Serampore, he translated the Bible into Bengali, Oriya, Marathi, Hindi, Assamese and Sanskrit, and parts of it into 29 other languages and dialects. The Bengali New Testament came out in 1801.
notes: Honest note: Carey himself rejected the claim that he alone translated the Bible into forty languages. Native speakers did much of the work.
sources: Christian Classics Ethereal Library, George Smith, *The Life of William Carey*, ch. 12

entries.title: Today: the full Bible in 795 languages
entries.body: The United Bible Societies count 795 languages with a full Bible, reaching about 6.2 billion people, out of 7,393 languages in total. In 2025 alone, translations were published in 100 languages spoken by about 566 million people. For 66 of those languages it was the first Scripture they had ever had. More than 1.5 billion people still have no full Bible in their own language, and the work goes on.
notes: Honest note: organisations count differently. These are UBS figures, and Wycliffe and ProgressBible publish their own.
sources: United Bible Societies, 2025 Translation Statistics Report (PDF)
Wycliffe Global Alliance, 2025 Scripture access statistics
